summary.text:
Liverpool's annual report contains the most significant single fact we have found about the inter-authority lending market this year. Paragraph 2.13: £118m of TERM borrowing arranged from seventeen different local authorities, average duration 2.7 years, average cost 4.49%. That is not cash management. It is a parallel funding market running at nearly the same scale as their PWLB programme — £118m against £114m of new PWLB — and it came in seven basis points cheaper than the 4.56% they paid the PWLB. Every other council we have read uses that market for overnight-to-twelve-month liquidity only.

The report reconciles well. Our PWLB file holds 49 loans at £734,555,556 against their £734.6m; the §2.10 debt table foots row by row and on both movement columns; the §2.12 new-borrowing table sums to £114,000,000 and reblends to 4.5565% against the stated 4.56%; and the balance sheet identity closes exactly in both years — CFR £1,114.3m less £944.1m of borrowing less £51.1m of PFI and other liabilities is the £119.1m of internal borrowing they print. Both performance indicators rebuild exactly too.

Paragraph 2.14 is unusually honest about the year end: £15m at 5.20% for seven days in Q4, with the reason given (a constrained market) and the mitigation stated (a week's money limits the impact) rather than buried in an average. Their Q2 borrowing at 4.15% is the same rate Gloucestershire got for its cheapest loan of the year.

And paragraphs 2.6 and 2.9 say what most reports will not: reserves drawn down to support revenue spending are shrinking the capacity to borrow internally, and 'the low level of reserves now places pressure to externalise the Council's borrowing in future years'. Internal borrowing already fell £22.6m. On today's repayment curve the book carries about £102.0m of net discount, so any externalising ahead would be done at rates well above the 3.34% the existing book costs. NO OFFICER ADDRESS is published anywhere in this appendix.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual report that went to Finance and Resources Scrutiny on 23 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 49 PWLB loans for Liverpool totalling £734,555,556, against the £734.6m in your paragraph 2.10 debt table. That table foots row by row and on both movement columns; your new-borrowing table at 2.12 sums to £114,000,000 and reblends to 4.5565% against the 4.56% you state; and the balance sheet closes exactly in both years — CFR £1,114.3m less £944.1m of borrowing less £51.1m of PFI and other liabilities is the £119.1m of internal borrowing you print, and the prior year does the same. Both of your Annex 1 performance indicators rebuild as well: 4.53% against a 4.51% one-year benchmark is the 0.02%, and 4.17% against a 4.01% SONIA is the 0.16%.

We wrote because of paragraph 2.13, which describes something we have not seen anywhere else.

£118m of term borrowing, from seventeen different local authorities, at an average duration of 2.7 years and an average cost of 4.49%. Alongside £114m of new PWLB at 4.56%.

We have now read the annual reports of some ninety councils, and every other one treats the inter-authority market as overnight-to-twelve-month liquidity — cash management, a way to avoid drawing PWLB for a few weeks. You used it as a substitute for medium-term PWLB, at nearly the same scale as your PWLB programme, and it came in seven basis points cheaper across a comparable duration. That is a different thing entirely, and as far as we can see nobody else is doing it at that size.

It is worth saying what the sector looks like from the other side of that trade, because it tells you something about where the 4.49% came from. Staffordshire's report names all twenty-five councils it lent to and shows its local authority book rising from £30m to £152m in a year. Gloucestershire borrowed £55m at 4.15% to 4.70%. At the other end, over the same year end, Cornwall paid 8.50% for four days and Bexley paid Herefordshire 7.00% for 32 days. So there is a lot of money looking for term counterparties and a very wide spread on short money, which is roughly the market you priced into. The distribution is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, alongside the monthly PWLB picture — July was thin, £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, and thin PWLB months are exactly when the short end of the LA market prices widest.

Which brings us to your paragraph 2.14, and this is a compliment. £15m at 5.20% for seven days in the fourth quarter, with the reason stated plainly — the market was constrained at the year end — and the mitigation stated just as plainly, that a week's money limits the impact. Most reports fold that sort of thing into an annual average and move on. Yours prints it by quarter with the durations, so a member can see that the 5.20% was seven days rather than seven months. For what it is worth your Q2 rate of 4.15% is the lowest inter-authority rate we have on record for the year, matched only by Gloucestershire.

The third thing is paragraphs 2.6 and 2.9, which we mention because they set up the question your 2.13 strategy will eventually meet. Reserves drawn down to support revenue spending reduce the capacity to borrow internally, and you say directly that the low level of reserves now places pressure to externalise borrowing in future years. Internal borrowing already fell £22.6m this year. The relevant number from our side is what externalising would cost against what the existing book costs: your PWLB portfolio has a weighted rate of 3.34%, and today's certainty curve on notice 314/26 is 4.95% at one year, 5.34% at five and 5.83% at ten. The same gap shows up as a discount if you look at it from the other end — 32 of your 49 loans price below par, for about £102.0m net.

We're not suggesting anything follows from that. We don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote a real figure. It is simply the arithmetic of the position your 2.9 describes, and yours is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit Liverpool. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets and LA Credit Analysis go straight to 2.13 and the seventeen lenders. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice and Reserves & balances strategy go to the externalising pressure in 2.6 and 2.9. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26 (Appendix 3), Finance and Resources Scrutiny Committee, 23 July 2026.
